book.title: Jazz Guitar Single Note Soloing, Vol 1
book.summary: Systematic chord-scale framework for jazz single-note soloing on guitar. Builds from the major scale as universal reference through numeric chord formulas, named chord groups (major Group 1; dominant Groups 1-4) paired with specific scales (Major, Lydian, Dominant 7th, Overtone/Lydian Dominant, Minor 7th, Altered Dominant Types 1/2/3). Method emphasizes 8th-note primacy, swing-and-straight practice, fingerboard visualization, position-based scale combining within a 5-6 fret area, hammer-on/pull-off/trill articulation constrained to scale tones, and root-based scale internalization (no relative-major shortcuts).

chapters.title: Getting Started
chapters.summary: Establishes the entire conceptual architecture of the method: the major scale as universal reference, numeric scale-degree notation, the chord formula system (every chord expressed as a numeric pattern over the major scale), the four triad types, upper partials (9/11/13), and the operational concept that a chord 'takes' a scale. Introduces the first concrete chord-scale rule: major Group 1 takes either the major scale or the Lydian scale.

sections.title: Single-Note Soloing defined & three core questions
sections.summary: Defines single-note soloing as playing successions of single notes forming melodies, and establishes the three-question framework — what notes sound good, where they are on the instrument, how to make them sound interesting — that organizes the entire pedagogical arc.

sections.title: Chord formula system & triad taxonomy
sections.summary: Defines chord tones, the chord formula system (every chord expressed as a numeric pattern over the major scale), the b/# notation convention (lower/raise by a half-step), and catalogues the four basic triad types: major (1,3,5), minor (1,b3,5), diminished (1,b3,b5), augmented (1,3,#5).

have a certain group of tones called a formula, that is derived from the major scale.

chapters.summary: Hands-on application chapter: drills basic theory + major-scale fingerings across positions. Predominantly notated exercises with no load-bearing prose; rules absorbed here are downstream applications of Chapter 1's framework (position practice of major scale).
chapters.skipped_reason: Chapter contains only notated exercises (major-scale fingerings); no load-bearing prose passages were identified at stage S2. Practice rules are inherited from the chapter-1 framework and the standing position-practice convention developed across chs.4-7.

chapters.title: Slurring & Decoration Part 1 / Tempo: 8ths, Triplets, 16ths, Double-timing
chapters.summary: Introduces the technical and rhythmic layer of the method. Establishes 8th notes as jazz's primary rhythmic unit; defines swing feel via triplet subdivision; introduces double-timing; lays down the standing rule that every 8th-note pattern be practiced in both swing and straight feel and that clean play precedes tempo increases. Then introduces slurring articulation: hammer-ons (constrained to scale tones at this stage), pull-offs, and the trill (framed as decoration of a held note rather than substitution). Closes the chapter with the Dominant 7th scale definition (major with b7) and the standing root-based-thinking rule against the relative-major shortcut.

sections.title: Tempo & rhythmic feels (8ths, swing, double-timing)
sections.summary: Establishes the eighth note as jazz's normal rhythmic unit at medium and fast tempos; defines swing 8ths via triplet subdivision with the middle note tied or missing; mandates practicing every run in both swing and straight feel; names and defines double-timing; states the clean-before-fast rule.

engine_rules.name: 8th note is the primary rhythmic unit for jazz single-note lines at medium and fast tempos
engine_rules.falsifier: A medium-tempo run written predominantly in quarter notes or dotted-quarter syncopations with no 8th-note backbone.
engine_rules.anchor:
the normal unit of
rhythm in jazz is the 8th note.

engine_rules.name: Swing 8ths are written-straight 8ths performed as triplet-subdivision with the middle of three tied/missing
engine_rules.falsifier: Performing 'swing 8ths' as literal even 8ths or as dotted-8th-plus-16th hard-shuffle — both diverge from the triplet-subdivision definition.
engine_rules.anchor:
each group of two 8th notes is actually played as if it were a group of three triplets,

with the middle one tied or missing.

engine_rules.name: Every 8th-note pattern must be practiced in both swing and straight feel
engine_rules.falsifier: Rehearsing a run only in swing because the chart marks 'swing' — both feels are required regardless of the tune's nominal feel.
engine_rules.anchor:
all the 8th notes in this book should be played as jazz 8ths and straight 8ths,
because both feels are necessary to today’s music.

engine_rules.name: Double-timing = 16th notes at medium-or-fast tempos as an advanced texture
engine_rules.falsifier: Calling 8th notes at a fast tempo 'double-timing' — double-timing specifically requires 16th-note subdivision over the prevailing beat.
engine_rules.anchor:
Players who possess great technique often love to break into 16th notes at medium (or even fast!)
tempos; this is commonly referred to as double-timing.

engine_rules.name: Achieve cleanliness at current tempo before increasing it
engine_rules.falsifier: Pushing a run from 120 to 140 bpm while still buzzing notes or mistiming the swing subdivision at 120.

cleanly at any tempo before moving on to a faster one.

sections.title: Slurring & decoration: hammer-ons, trills
sections.summary: Constrains hammer-on targets to tones inside the active scale at this stage of study; positions isolated hammer-ons as not-yet-standard jazz devices (the grace-note exception is deferred to Vol. II) and frames them as building blocks for the trill. chapters.title: The Dominant 7th Scale: Group-1/Group-2 Dominants, Combining Scales in One Position
chapters.summary: Develops the dominant scale layer: subdivides dominants into Group 1 (no 11th — runs should contain the 3rd) and Group 2 (with 11th — runs should contain the 11th); teaches that register governs how extensions like b7 and 9 are perceived; introduces position-based 'combining scales in one position' for multi-chord soloing within a 5-6 fret area; reaffirms fingerboard visualization as the primary internalization technique. Introduces the Minor 7th scale (major with b3, b7), prohibits the relative-major shortcut for it, and situates m7 study within the ii-V-I progression. Closes with the Overtone Dominant scale (dominant 7th with #4) and a Jazz Waltz creative-application aside.

sections.title: Group-1 / Group-2 dominants & run-group synchronization
sections.summary: States that register is the variable that makes b7 and 9 'come alive' as spicy lower-mid notes rather than weighty bass tones. Gives the synchronization rule: a run containing the 3rd suits Group-1 dominants; a run containing the 11th suits Group-2 dominants; runs containing both or neither work over either group (with care about lingering tones).

group-2 dominants.

chapters.title: The Minor 7th Scale & Altered Dominant Foundations
chapters.summary: Develops the minor 7th and altered dominant layers. Names the Overtone Dominant as also known as Lydian Dominant; identifies the upper-structure triad on Lydian/Lydian-Dominant scales (9, #11, 13 forming a major triad a whole step above the root) and names polytonality as the resulting device. Defines an altered dominant scale as any Dominant 7th scale containing b9, #9, b5 or #5/b13; groups all such chords as GROUP 4 DOMINANT CHORDS; explicitly excludes Overtone Dominant from the altered class (its #11 is from the overtone series, not chromatic alteration). Introduces the package-deal pedagogical method (all three altered-type scales taught side by side in one position) and the remedial rule that returning to chord forms resolves visualization difficulty.

sections.title: Lydian Dominant, upper-structure triad & polytonality

Identifies the upper-structure triad (9, #11, 13 forming a major triad rooted a whole step above the chord) as the 'hippest' polytonal device of both Lydian and Lydian Dominant scales. Names polytonality as the underlying concept (forward-referenced to a full Vol II chapter).

sections.title: Altered dominant scales & Group 4 dominants
sections.summary: Defines an altered dominant scale as any Dominant 7th scale with one or more of b9, #9, b5, or #5/b13. Establishes that any dominant chord containing one or more of these altered tones is a Group 4 dominant. Critically excludes Overtone Dominant from the altered class: its #11 reflects the overtone series, not chromatic alteration.

engine_rules.name: Altered dominant scale = Dominant 7th scale with one or more of b9, #9, b5, #5/b13
engine_rules.falsifier: Calling a scale 'altered dominant' when its only modification of the dominant 7th scale is a #11 — that's Overtone Dominant, not altered.
engine_rules.anchor:
What is an altered dominant scale? Simply, any dominant 7th scale with one or
more of the following tones: 59, #9, 65 or #5 (613).

engine_rules.name: Group 4 dominants = any dominant 7th type chord containing one or more altered tones
engine_rules.falsifier: Placing a 7#11 chord (no altered b9/#9/b5/#5) into Group 4 — it belongs in Group 3 (Overtone Dominant).
engine_rules.anchor:
Any Dom. 7th type chord that contains any one or more of the four altered tones (69, #9, 65 and
#5 or 613) will be considered as being part of what we call the GROUP 4 DOMINANT CHORDS.

sections.title: Package-deal pedagogy & visualization remediation
sections.summary: States the pedagogical method of presenting all three altered-type scales side by side in the same fingerboard position so subtle color differences are absorbed comparatively. Sets a remedial rule: when runs are hard to visualize, return to the position's chord forms first.

engine_rules.name: Teach related altered-dominant scales side by side in one position for comparative absorption
engine_rules.falsifier: Drilling Type 1 in position 1, then moving to a completely different position for Type 2 — denies comparative absorption.
engine_rules.anchor:
the three types of A.D. scales are all so
similar that your brain, while noting the differences, can absorb them all in a kind of ‘package deal’, one
position at a time.

engine_rules.name: When runs are hard to visualize, return to chord forms in that position first
engine_rules.falsifier: Drilling the same run pattern faster as a remedy for failing to visualize it — book prescribes going back to the chord forms, not increasing repetition tempo.
engine_rules.anchor: If you have trouble visualizing any of these runs, then please, for your own good, go back and learn the chord forms (group 4) for this position.

sections.title: Standing chord-substitution allowances & practice rules
sections.summary: Standing substitution rule for Type 3 pages: A7+ may stand in for A7#9+, and D49 may stand in for D6/9. Standing practice rule: try every run an octave higher within the same position. Performance rule: the altered #9 can substitute for or supplement the natural 9. Structural boundary: there's no Type 3 - 4A on guitar — instrument geometry forbids it. Higher-register arpeggios provided as supplements.
